# Volume 3 — Chapter XIV The Summons

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Opal Pettigrew and Nell were seated in the Pettigrews’ garden when the day, having dragged itself slowly across the space, finally vanished. A warm, smoky afternoon of summer had just passed. Outbursts of blooms covered the earth in magnificence. Hazes filled the lazy valleys. Shadows decorated the paths through the woods, while purple asters adorned the fields.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0000 }

Nell had sacrificed a night excursion under the moon to the Pale Sands beach so that Opal could have her company for the evening. Throughout that summer, she had passed numerous evenings in the same manner, even though she frequently questioned the benefit it brought to anybody, and occasionally returned home resolved never to return.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0001 }

As the summer drew to a close, Opal’s complexion became paler; she surrendered the Pale Sands school—“till New Year’s, her father believed she ought not to teach”—and the fancy work she cherished slipped from her hands with increasing frequency as they became too tired to hold it. Nevertheless, she remained perpetually cheerful, ever optimistic, constantly talking and whispering about her suitors, alongside their conflicts and heartbreaks. Because of this, Nell found her visits difficult to endure. What previously appeared foolish or entertaining had turned macabre; it resembled death gazing out from behind a deliberate facade of vitality. Even so, Opal appeared to hold fast to her, refusing to allow her to depart without a pledge to return shortly. Mrs. Sowerby complained regarding how often Nell visited, asserting that she would contract consumption, and even Thirza felt uncertain.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0002 }

“Each time you visit Opal you return looking exhausted,” she said.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0003 }

“It is extremely mournful and terrible,” Nell stated quietly. “Opal appears completely unaware of her state. Even so, I somehow sense her need for assistance—her longing for it—and I wish to provide it to her but am unable to. Whenever I am beside her, I feel just like I am observing her battle an unseen enemy—attempting to repel it using what little strength she possesses. This reason explains why I return home exhausted.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0004 }

However, Nell was not as acutely aware of this on this particular night. Opal remained unusually silent. Not a single word escaped her lips regarding dresses, drives, parties, and “fellows.” With her untouched work lying next to her, she rested in the hammock, a white shawl enveloped around her thin shoulders. Her lengthy yellow hair braids—those gorgeous braids that Nell used to envy so much during their former schooldays!—were positioned on both sides of her. She had removed the pins because they caused her head to ache, according to her. For the moment, the hectic flush had faded, causing her to appear pale and childlike.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0005 }

Ascending into the silver-hued sky, the moon gave a pearly luster to the surrounding clouds. Beneath it, the pond gleamed within that misty glow. Located a short distance past the Pettigrew homestead stood the church, accompanied by the ancient graveyard adjacent to it. Beaming upon the white stones, the moonlight rendered them vividly distinct against the backdrop of dark trees.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0006 }

“The cemetery appears so peculiar under the moon’s light!” Opal uttered abruptly. “So spectral!” she trembled. “Nell, the time is drawing near when I will be resting in that place. You, Isolde, and everyone else will be moving around, brimming with vitality—while I will be situated there—within the ancient cemetery—deceased!”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0007 }

Nell was thrown into confusion by the suddenness of the event. Speech eluded her for a brief period of time.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0008 }

“You are aware that it is true, aren’t you?” Opal urged.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0009 }

“Yes, I know,” Nell replied softly. “Dear Opal, I know.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0010 }

“Everyone is aware of it,” Opal stated with bitterness. “It is known to me—it has been known to me the entire summer, even if I refused to admit it. And, oh, Nell”—she stretched her hand forth and grasped the hand of Nell in a pleading, impulsive manner—“dying is not what I want. The thought of dying frightens me.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0011 }

“Opal, what is the reason for your fear?” Nell inquired in a soft voice.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0012 }

“Because—because—oh, Nell, I am not scared that I will fail to get into heaven. I belong to the church. But—everything there is going to be so unfamiliar. I ponder—and ponder—and it makes me so scared—and—and—homesick. Of course, heaven has to be extremely beautiful, as the Bible states—however, Nell, it will not be like what I am accustomed to.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0013 }

A unwelcome memory floated into Nell’s mind of an amusing tale she had listened to Cressida Lindsay recount—the narrative of a certain elderly man who had uttered almost the identical remark regarding the afterlife. At the time, it had struck her as comical—she recalled the way she and Honora had giggled about it. Yet, emanating from Opal’s wan, quivering lips, it did not appear the least bit funny anymore. It felt sorrowful, disastrous—and accurate! The celestial realm could not resemble what Opal was accustomed to. Absolutely nothing in her merry, lighthearted existence, nor her superficial principles and desires, had prepared her for that monumental transition, or rendered the next life as anything to her except foreign, imaginary, and unwanted. Powerlessly, Nell pondered what words of assistance she might offer her. Was there anything she could voice? “I think, Opal,” she initiated with uncertainty—since Nell found it challenging to converse with anyone about the profoundest reflections in her soul, or the fresh notions regarding the vast enigmas of existence in this world and the next that had indistinctly started forming in her thoughts, replacing her previous youthful beliefs, and talking about them to someone like Opal Pettigrew was the most difficult of all—“I think, perhaps, we have very mistaken ideas about heaven—what it is and what it holds for us. I don’t think it can be so very different from life here as most people seem to think. I believe we’ll just go on living, a good deal as we live here—and be ourselves just the same—only it will be easier to be good and to—follow the highest. All the hindrances and perplexities will be taken away, and we shall see clearly. Don’t be afraid, Opal.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0014 }

“I can’t help it,” Opal said in a pitiful manner. “Even if what you say about heaven is true—and you can’t be sure—it may be only that imagination of yours—it won’t be just the same. It can’t be. I want to go on living here. I’m so young, Nell. I haven’t had my life. I’ve fought so hard to live—and it isn’t any use—I have to die—and leave everything I care for.” Nell remained seated, experiencing an agony that was nearly unbearable. She was unable to utter soothing lies; and every word Opal spoke was so dreadfully accurate. She was departing from all she held dear. It was on earth alone that she had stored her treasures; she had existed entirely for the small matters of life—the things that fade away—neglecting the grand matters that proceed into eternity, spanning the chasm between the two existences and turning death into a simple transition from a single abode to another—from dusk to clear daylight. There, God would mind her—Nell believed—she would come to understand—yet at present it was not surprising that her soul held fast, with unseeing helplessness, to the sole items she understood and cherished.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0015 }

Prop scene on her arm, Opal elevated her luminous, lovely blue eyes toward the heavens bathed in moonlight.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0016 }

“I want to live,” she said, her voice shaking. “I want to live the way other girls do. I—I desire to get married, Nell—and—and—possess tiny children. You are aware that babies were always something I loved, Nell. To nobody else except you could I admit this. That you comprehend, I know. Furthermore, poor Herb—he—he cares for me and my love belongs to him, Nell. Nothing was meant to me by the others, yet he matters—and provided I could remain alive, I would become his wife and experience such happiness. Oh, Nell, this is difficult.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0017 }

Reclining once more upon her pillows, Opal wept uncontrollably. Nell squeezed her hand with immense, anguished empathy—a voiceless compassion that may have comforted Opal better than fragmented, flawed speech ever could; consequently, her agitation soon waned and her weeping stopped.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0018 }

“I am pleased that I have shared this with you, Nell,” she murmured. “Simply expressing everything has brought me relief. Throughout the entire summer—with each of your visits—I desired to do so. I wished to discuss it with you—yet it was impossible for me. Admitting my impending demise, or having another person utter or imply it, felt as though it would render death absolute. I refused to speak it, or allow myself to contemplate it. During daylight hours, surrounded by others and amidst bright surroundings, avoiding such thoughts proved less difficult. However, during sleepless nights—Nell, it was utterly terrible. Escape from it was impossible at those times. Death merely arrived and gazed directly at me, terrifying me to the point where I felt ready to shriek.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0019 }

“However, Opal, you will not feel scared from now on, will you? You are going to be courageous, and have faith that everything will turn out fine for you.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0020 }

“I will endeavor to do so. What you told me will be weighed in my mind, and I will attempt to hold it as true. Also, your visits will be as frequent as possible, will they not, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0021 }

“Certainly, my love.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0022 }

“It—it will not take much time now, Nell. I am certain of that. And I would prefer to have you over anybody else. Of all the girls I attended school alongside, I always favored you the most. You never showed jealousy, or malice, as a few of them did. Poor Em White came by to visit me yesterday. Do you recall that Em and I were great friends for three years while attending school? And subsequently we fell out at the time of the school concert. Ever since, we have not uttered a word to one another. Was it not foolish? Any occurrence of that sort appears foolish at present. However, Em and I resolved the former dispute yesterday. She mentioned that she would have conversed years back, except she believed I would refuse to. And I refrained from ever conversing with her since I was convinced she would refuse to converse with me. Is it not peculiar the way folks misjudge one another, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0023 }

“It seems to me that the majority of life’s difficulties arise from a lack of understanding,” Nell stated. “I have to leave at this moment, Opal. The hour is growing late—and staying out in this moisture is bad for you.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0024 }

“It will not be long before you ascend once more.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0025 }

“Yes, extremely shortly. And I will be delighted if I can assist you in any way.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0026 }

“I am aware. Already, you have provided aid to me. At present, nothing appears entirely so terrible. Good night, Nell.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0027 }

“Good night, my love.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0028 }

Nell made her way back home with great deliberation under the light of the moon. Something within her had been altered by the evening. The significance of life was now different, its intention more profound. Externally, everything would proceed as before; nevertheless, her innermost depths had been moved. Her fate could not resemble that of poor butterfly Opal. Arriving at the conclusion of one existence could not mean encountering the subsequent one with the recoil of fear toward an entirely alien realm—a realm for which habitual ideas, thoughts, and ambitions had left her unready. The minor details of existence, while pleasant and fine in their proper context, could not become her reasons for living; she had to seek out and pursue the ultimate; the existence of heaven had to commence right here in this earthly world.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0029 }

That lovely evening in the garden was forever. Opal was never again seen alive by Nell. The following night a send-off party was held by the B.V.I.S. for Odette Pullen prior to her leaving for the West. And, as light feet were dancing and bright eyes were laughing and merry tongues were chattering, a call came to a soul in Brierley that could neither be ignored nor avoided. The following morning news spread from one house to another that Opal Pettigrew had passed away. She had passed away in her sleep, without pain and peacefully, bearing a smile on her face—as though, in the end, death had arrived like a gentle friend guiding her across the doorway, rather than the horrific specter she had feared.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0030 }

Following the burial, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby stated with conviction that Opal Pettigrew was the most beautiful deceased person she had ever beheld. Dressed in white amidst the fragile blossoms Nell had arranged around her, her physical grace while resting was recalled and discussed in Brierley for a long time. Opal’s attractiveness had been constant; however, her charm had possessed a worldly, grounded nature that carried a specific arrogant air, seeming to display itself boldly to any viewer, unilluminated by soul and unpolished by mind. Yet the touch of death had hallowed her features, revealing subtle contours and a faultless silhouette hitherto invisible—achieving what living, loving, profound grief, and the intense happiness of womanhood might have accomplished for Opal. Gazing through her blurred weeping at her former companion, Nell believed she observed the countenance God had intended for Opal, keeping that image in her mind forever.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0031 }

Prior to the departure of the funeral procession from the house, Mrs. Pettigrew drew Nell into an empty room and handed her a small package.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0032 }

“Take this, I want it to be yours,” she wept. “Having you possess it is what Opal would have wanted. This embroidered centerpiece was a project she was making. A little work remains—where her poor small fingers left it when she set it aside for the final time, during the afternoon preceding her death, the needle still pierces the fabric.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0033 }

“A portion of incomplete labor is perpetually remaining,” Mrs. Sowerby remarked, her eyes filled with tears. “Yet I imagine an individual is constantly present to complete it.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0034 }

“It is so hard to truly grasp that someone we have known forever is actually gone,” Nell remarked while she and Isolde made their way back home. “Opal is the very first among our schoolmates to pass away. Eventually, one after another, every single one of us will have to follow.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0035 }

“Yes, I suppose so,” Isolde stated with discomfort. Talking about that was not what she desired. Discussing the particulars of the funeral—the magnificent white velvet coffin Mr. Pettigrew had demanded for Opal—“the Gillises must always make a splurge, even at funerals,” Mrs. Agatha Sowerby had remarked—the sorrowful countenance of Herb Tranter, the uninhibited, hysterical sorrow of a sister of Opal's—would have been her preference, yet Nell refused to converse about those matters. A daydream appeared to envelop her, one in which Isolde felt with loneliness that she shared no portion or role.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0036 }

“A great girl to laugh was Opal Pettigrew,” Robin remarked all at once. “Is she going to laugh in heaven as frequently as she did in Brierley, Nell? I wish to know.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0037 }

“Indeed, I believe she is going to,” Nell remarked.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0038 }

“Oh, Nell,” Isolde objected, smiling in a somewhat scandalized way.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0039 }

“Well, why not, Isolde?” Nell inquired with gravity. “Is it your belief that we will never laugh in heaven?”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0040 }

“Oh—I—I do not know” stumbled Isolde. “It appears not quite proper, in some way. You are aware that it is quite terrible to giggle inside a church.”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0041 }

“However, church is not what heaven will resemble—continuously,” Nell stated.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0042 }

“I trust it isn’t,” Robin stated with force. “Should it be, I have no desire to attend. Church is terribly boring. Regardless, I do not intend on going for a very long time. My intention is to reach one hundred years of age, similar to Mr. Thomas Scobie of Pale Sands. He claims his longevity is due to always smoking tobacco, which destroyed every germ. Will I be allowed to smoke tobacco fairly soon, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0043 }

“No, Robin, my wish is that tobacco will never be used by you,” Nell remarked in a distracted manner.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0044 }

“How will it make you feel if I end up dying from the germs, in that case?” Robin asked.
{: #nw-v03-c14-p0045 }
